title: the machine's slot queue, readable and reorderable from anything on the wire
asserts: a core that advertises `heavyQueue` lets a client that is not the Mac see what is holding the shared `heavy` slots, move a job in line, widen the queue and cancel a job. The queue is not this core's state - it is a directory three other processes are writing, and the wrappers admit themselves from it - so `heavyQueueSubscribe` is answered with the whole queue read NOW rather than with whatever the last change happened to be, and every mutation is answered by the queue again, complete and never a delta, because a client that applied a patch to a registry somebody else also writes would diverge from the line the wrappers are actually using. Reordering is a priority rewrite and nothing else: higher runs sooner, ties break on how long a job has been queued, and a core that answered a nudge by reordering its own copy would be a second opinion about who runs next. The two refusals are the load-bearing half. `heavySetSlots` below one slot is refused rather than clamped, because a queue that admits nothing forever is not a narrower queue. `heavyCancel` for a pid this queue does not hold is refused rather than signalled, which is what keeps the frame from being an arbitrary-signal gadget aimed at any process on the machine by anything that can reach this socket - the check is membership in the core's own snapshot, so the worst a client can do is stop a job that is in the list it was just sent. And an unsubscribe really stops the frames, because the core reads the shared registry only while somebody is watching.

steps.note: the registry is seeded by the boot (JUANCODE_HEAVY_ROOT), because a scenario cannot write a file and a core pointed at the real /tmp/claude-heavy-$UID would be reordering the developer's own jobs

the whole queue, read now. Capacity with no config file is the wrapper's own default (1 slot, 4 workers) - reported rather than invented, so a client never disagrees with the shell script about what the capacity is. Both jobs are waiting and equally prioritised, so the order is age: A was queued before B
the only mutation the line has. The waiting wrapper re-reads its own entry every poll and admits itself from it, so a number in that file is the only thing anybody can change about the order
answered by the queue rather than by a reply of its own, and the whole queue: the registry has other writers, so a delta a client applied to its own copy would drift from the line the wrappers read
capacity is state, not a knob that only applies to new jobs: the waiting wrappers re-read it every poll, so raising it lets jobs already in line through
and the worker cap is untouched, because widening the queue must not rewrite the other keys in the wrapper's config - the rules in it belong to the wrapper and are read by other tooling
refused rather than clamped: a client that asked for zero gets told, instead of silently getting one

the refusal this whole frame rests on. A pid the core's own snapshot does not hold is not the core's to signal - without that check the frame is an arbitrary-signal gadget, and 0 in particular is the core's own process group
the capacity back where the boot left it, so a second attempt in the same run reads the same queue this one started from
and the line back to the order the boot seeded, for the same reason - and this one doubles as the assertion below: the reorder really happens, it is just not sent to a client that stopped watching
longer than the core's own registry poll, so silence here is an unsubscribe that took effect rather than a tick that had not come round yet
and re-subscribing proves the mutation above landed while nobody was listening: the queue is read from the registry, not replayed from a stream
